_purpose: GOAT calibration corpus (en). Hand-authored expectations for the WHOLE pipeline: classify() intent + parse() slots. Seeded from .superpowers/research/en-expressions.md (162 rows), crossed systematically over {amount form} x {pay verb} x {split form} x {noise}, and extended with every English sentence this branch's review rounds argued about.
_howToRead: payer/participants name members; 'actor' is the person typing. A row with a `known` field is a PINNED MISS: `expect` records today's behavior and `known` says why it is not fixed. Never weaken a row to make it pass — fix the parser, or pin it with a justification.

rows.known: cent/cents is not in CURRENCY_WORDS_EN, and adding it there would be WRONG: that map takes a word to an ISO code, with no way to say the word also names the MINOR unit, so 99 cents would come back as 99 USD instead of 0.99. Sub-dollar amounts stay null (the UI asks) until the lexicon can carry a scale — a schema change, not a lexicon row. $0.99 for the app reads correctly.

rows.known: MANDATED (T8) as a description row: `with` here governs `cash`, not a name, so nothing binds it and it survives as a one-word description — cosmetic, and visible on the card. The INTENT is also a miss: the query ladder's MY_SPENDING AND-group is firstPerson + paidVerb, which this statement matches word for word (`I` + `paid`) even though it asks nothing. Requiring an interrogative marker across the whole query ladder is a classify-wide change with its own pinned corpus, out of scope for calibration.

rows.known: `no split` is a real English way to say this expense is not shared, and nothing in the split lexicon negates a split expression — the word `split` itself matches and reads as everyone. Negation over the split vocabulary is a grammar the parser does not have; the participants are visible and editable on the confirm card.

`X is out` (an exclusion) is not in the participant vocabulary, so Sam is read as a PARTICIPANT rather than excluded — the opposite of what the sentence says. `everyone but Sam` and `without Alex` are the supported forms; both are attested and both work. The card shows the participant pills, which is where this is caught.

rows.known: Banknote nicknames (a fiver, a tenner, a Benjamin, a sawbuck) are attested but absent from the English money vocabulary; each names a currency AND a value, which the current lexicon shape (word -> ISO code) cannot express — `a fiver` would have to carry the value 5, not just GBP/USD. Null keeps the UI asking instead of inventing.

rows.known: The spoken price form `twelve fifty` (= 12.50) is not read: the number grammar composes tiers, so `twelve fifty` would have to mean 62 or 1250 before it could mean 12.50, and every one of those readings is a confidently wrong amount. Null asks instead.

rows.known: A STATEMENT built out of the balance question's own words ("I owe") is read as the question. The query ladder is keyword AND-groups, not a mood analysis, and every attested D-1 row is exactly this shape minus the trailing number. The reply is a balance readout — unhelpful rather than harmful — and separating statements from questions is a classify-wide change with its own pinned corpus. Same class as "I paid with cash".

rows.note: Fix round 2 ruling: a field-named amount modify reads the number ONLY when the amount parser agrees it is money. 3명 / 3 people is a headcount, so the slot stays null and the card asks — the loose fragment reader on its own would have set the amount to 3.

Fix round 2, controller ruling: `total` is money vocabulary in this domain, so it joins the money-CONFIRMING followers that override the year rule. It was refused while the identical shape outside the band ("dinner 12000 total", a row above) read correctly — an inconsistency, not a conservative choice. Held to `total` alone; altogether/sum stay out until the corpus asks.

Fix round 3 ruling: `went`, `going` and `all` are only the first words of the split PHRASES "went dutch" / "going dutch" / "all together", and on their own they confirm nothing — so they are dropped from the money-confirming set and the year rule stands here.

rows.known: The stated cost of keeping `everyone` in the money-confirming set (fix round 3): it overrides the year rule, so a year followed by `everyone` reads as an amount. It stays because a number followed by `everyone` is an expense entry ("dinner 1500 everyone") far more often than it is a sentence about a year, and the three first-words that confirm NOTHING (all/went/going) were dropped instead. 0.6 confidence, card-visible.

The other side of the same ruling: "all together" IS a split phrase, but its first word `all` was dropped from the money-confirming set, so a price in the year band followed by it is refused. Outside the band it is unaffected ("lunch 3000 all together evenly" reads 3000, a frozen test). Matching whole phrases here instead would fix it; the ruling chose the smaller change.

The year band reaches into the card-reply path, because the field-named licence asks `parse()` — which carries its own disqualifiers — whether the fragment is money. 2000 with `please` after it is not, so the slot comes back null and the card asks "how much?", and the next message ("2000") is a fragment that resolves outright. One extra round trip, accepted: the alternative is a second, looser definition of money living in the classifier and disagreeing with the parser. "change the amount to $2000" and "change the amount to 2000 total" both resolve directly.

rows.note: The same year-band amount WITH a money-confirming follower resolves directly — the parser agrees, so the licence is taken.
